source: Dageville et al., "The Snowflake Elastic Data Warehouse", SIGMOD
relevance_note: Describes separated storage/compute and elastic virtual warehouses, the cost model Aurora would pay under a warehouse option.

source: Armbrust, Ghodsi, Xin, Zaharia, "Lakehouse: A New Generation of Open Platforms that Unify Data Warehousing and Advanced Analytics", CIDR
relevance_note: Core argument for a lakehouse: one copy of data serving BI and ML; authors are Databricks founders, so read alongside E-WL-01.

source: Armbrust et al., "Delta Lake: High-Performance ACID Table Storage over Cloud Object Stores", PVLDB 13(12)
relevance_note: Shows ACID tables on object storage, the mechanism that lets the ML team read features without an export copy.

source: Jain, Kraft, Power, Das, Stoica, Zaharia, "Analyzing and Comparing Lakehouse Storage Systems", CIDR
relevance_note: Compares Delta Lake, Hudi and Iceberg; relevant if the lakehouse option is chosen and a table format must be picked.

source: van Renen and Leis, "Cloud Analytics Benchmark", PVLDB 16(6)
relevance_note: Argues TPC-style benchmarks misrepresent real cloud BI workloads (many small, repetitive queries), which is Aurora's dashboard pattern.

source: Databricks, "Databricks Sets Official Data Warehousing Performance Record"
relevance_note: Claims TPC-DS 100 TB price/performance lead; Aurora's high scenario is ~1 TB, so headline numbers do not transfer.

source: Snowflake, "Industry Benchmarks and Competing with Integrity"
relevance_note: Snowflake's rebuttal to E-WL-06; useful mainly as a reminder that vendor benchmarks are contested and tuned.

source: Fivetran (G. Fraser), "Cloud Data Warehouse Benchmark"
relevance_note: Third-party TPC-DS comparison of Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift, Databricks and Synapse with default settings; closest public analogue to a small team's untuned setup.

source: ClickHouse Inc., "ClickBench: a Benchmark for Analytical DBMS"
relevance_note: Open, reproducible results on a 100M-row web-analytics table similar in shape to Aurora clickstream; maintained by a competing vendor.

source: Aurora PoC: retention marts + feature extract on two shortlisted platforms
relevance_note: Only source that reflects Aurora's query mix, concurrency, data size and negotiated pricing.

source: Sculley et al., "Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems", NeurIPS
relevance_note: Identifies pipeline jungles and glue code as ML debt; motivates a single orchestrated path from marts to churn features.

source: Foidl, Golendukhina, Ramler, Felderer, "Data pipeline quality: Influencing factors, root causes of data-related issues, and processing problem areas for developers", Journal of Systems and Software
relevance_note: Catalogues root causes of pipeline data issues; informs which quality checks the orchestrator must enforce.

source: Breck, Cai, Nielsen, Salib, Sculley, "The ML Test Score: A Rubric for ML Production Readiness and Technical Debt Reduction", IEEE BigData
relevance_note: Defines data and feature tests the hand-off to the ML team should satisfy; orchestration must schedule and gate them.

source: Dagster Labs, "Introducing Software-Defined Assets"
relevance_note: Pitches asset-centric orchestration with built-in lineage; relevant to whether data-product ownership maps to assets rather than tasks.

source: Astronomer, "State of Apache Airflow" report
relevance_note: Adoption and usage survey run by the main commercial Airflow vendor; signals hiring pool and ecosystem maturity, not fitness for Aurora.

source: dbt Labs, "State of Analytics Engineering"
relevance_note: Practitioner survey on tooling and pain points (data quality, ownership); vendor-run, but reflects the analytics-engineering team profile Aurora will hire.

source: Aurora pilot: 12-month backfill + seeded-fault drill on shortlisted orchestrators
relevance_note: Backfill time, fault detection and team onboarding effort depend on Aurora's DAG size and staff; no external source covers them.

source: Zaharia et al., "Discretized Streams: Fault-Tolerant Streaming Computation at Scale", SOSP
relevance_note: Foundational micro-batch model; shows seconds-level latency is achievable without a true streaming engine.

source: Akidau et al., "The Dataflow Model", PVLDB 8(12)
relevance_note: Frames the correctness/latency/cost trade-off explicitly; the vocabulary for justifying the chosen freshness SLA.

source: Armbrust et al., "Structured Streaming: A Declarative API for Real-Time Applications in Apache Spark", SIGMOD
relevance_note: Shows a single API can run as micro-batch or continuous, reducing the cost of starting with micro-batch and upgrading later.

source: Chintapalli et al., "Benchmarking Streaming Computation Engines: Storm, Flink and Spark Streaming", IEEE IPDPSW
relevance_note: Yahoo ad-event benchmark of latency vs throughput; event rates far exceed Aurora's ~435 events/s peak-day average.

source: Karimov et al., "Benchmarking Distributed Stream Data Processing Systems", ICDE
relevance_note: Rigorous latency-measurement methodology; reuse it when Aurora load-tests its own pipeline.

source: Kreps, "Benchmarking Apache Kafka: 2 Million Writes Per Second (On Three Cheap Machines)", LinkedIn Engineering
relevance_note: Shows ingest capacity is not the constraint at Aurora's volume; the decision is about cost and freshness, not throughput.

source: Databricks, "Project Lightspeed: Faster and Simpler Stream Processing with Apache Spark"
relevance_note: Vendor latency claims for Structured Streaming; useful for upper-bound expectations if the lakehouse path is chosen.

source: Snowflake, Snowpipe Streaming and Dynamic Tables documentation
relevance_note: Vendor-stated ingest latency and refresh lag; relevant if the warehouse path is chosen and micro-batch stays in-warehouse.

source: Aurora analysis: churn-signal-to-cancellation lag + pipeline load test
relevance_note: Whether sub-minute freshness changes retention outcomes depends entirely on Aurora customer behavior and intervention playbooks.

source: Lewis et al., "Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks", NeurIPS
relevance_note: Origin of the RAG pattern underpinning the retention-support assistant.

source: Shuster et al., "Retrieval Augmentation Reduces Hallucination in Conversation", Findings of EMNLP
relevance_note: Evidence that grounding on retrieved text reduces fabricated statements in dialogue, the main risk for a customer-facing assistant.

source: Liu et al., "Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts", TACL
relevance_note: Shows answer quality depends on where evidence sits in context; argues for tight top-k retrieval over stuffing transcripts.

source: Yao et al., "ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models", ICLR
relevance_note: Basis for tool-using agent loops; the agentic option would extend RAG with account lookups and offer actions.

source: Es, James, Espinosa-Anke, Schockaert, "RAGAS: Automated Evaluation of Retrieval Augmented Generation", EACL (demo)
relevance_note: Provides faithfulness and context-relevance metrics Aurora can use in its own evaluation harness.

source: Muennighoff, Tazi, Magne, Reimers, "MTEB: Massive Text Embedding Benchmark", EACL
relevance_note: Shortlists embedding models; general-domain rankings may not hold on support-ticket language.

relevance_note: Customer-service agent benchmark (retail, airline) with pass^k reliability; shows agents are inconsistent across repeated trials.

relevance_note: Shows many agent benchmarks ignore cost; supports evaluating accuracy and cost jointly before choosing agentic over workflow.

source: Anthropic, "Building Effective Agents"
relevance_note: Model vendor recommends starting with simple workflows and adding agent autonomy only when it measurably helps.

relevance_note: Retrieval quality, hallucination rate, PII leakage and cost must be measured on Aurora transcripts and policies.
